title: Everyday Sensory Experiences of Autistic University Students in Australia: An Experience Sampling Approach.
abstract: Sensory differences and discomfort are significant on-campus barriers for many autistic postsecondary students, but we know relatively little about what makes sensory environments accessible or inaccessible for autistic students. In this study, 19 autistic university students in Australia answered experience sampling questions thrice daily for 2 weeks. Quantitative sensory comfort ratings were significantly poorer when participants reported states of greater anxiety, irritability, emotional reactivity and exhaustion. Participants also reported more quantitative sensory discomfort when open-ended answers described feeling tired/exhausted, anxious or stressed/overwhelmed, rather than feeling relaxed/good. Our study cannot resolve the causality of these relationships. Notably, however, between-person trait differences in anxiety, irritability and exhaustion were not statistically related to sensory comfort. Qualitative-quantitative triangulation suggested that participants experienced less sensory comfort: in open-access spaces (notably, on campus, travelling and shopping) compared to closed-access spaces (notably, at home); to high-intensity (e.g., loud) than low-intensity (e.g., quiet) or non-notable stimulation; to most sounds over visual, feel and taste stimuli; to people-related sounds than touch sensations; and to crowds over environments with fewer people. These findings suggest sensory environments systematically shape many autistic people's everyday experiences and thus that we should modify these environments to be more accessible and inclusive.
